subsystem.name: canary
subsystem.note: The item 10 routing rehearsal, interlock tests/canary, 6 files. One ledger per source file. Not to be confused with parity/measurement.canary.ledger.json, which ports tests/measurement/test_canary.py -- the measurement harness's view of a canary, not the canary's own store. The two names sit next to each other in parity/ and mean different things.

file.note: The inventory is `pytest --collect-only -q` on the source at 65f36c5, in collection order; all 27 pass there (measured 2026-08-28 against the shared read-only clone of interlock at 65f36c5, `PYTHONPATH=src PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python3 -m pytest -q tests/canary/ -p no:cacheprovider`: 70 passed, of which 27 are tests/canary/test_ledger.py's).

systematic_mappings.why: better-sqlite3 raises one error type for everything and carries the distinction in `.code` (D-0016). The whole SQLITE_CONSTRAINT family is used, not one member, because `sqlite3.IntegrityError` covers RAISE(ABORT) (SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER), CHECK, UNIQUE and PRIMARYKEY without distinguishing them -- naming one would assert more than the source does. Where the source has a `match=`, it is kept alongside the code; where it has none (5 cases), none was added.
systematic_mappings.affects: All 16 ported cases that expect a store-level refusal.

systematic_mappings.why: Keeps both halves pytest asserts (the class AND a regex search over the message). Vitest's `toThrow` drops one half depending on which overload is reached for.
systematic_mappings.affects: The 10 ported cases raising RoutingLedgerRefusal / MissingLedgerRefused / CorruptLedgerRefused.

systematic_mappings.why: better-sqlite3 runs in autocommit, so a statement is durable when it returns. The source's `with ledger:` blocks (the two insert helpers) ARE transactions and are translated as `ledger.transaction(...)()`, which rolls back and rethrows exactly as the context manager does.
systematic_mappings.affects: The two helpers and 5 cases that call commit() explicitly before closing.

systematic_mappings.to: plain per-test functions `ledgerPath()` / `ledgerFixture()`, with the close registered by `onTestFinished` at acquisition
systematic_mappings.why: Conventions rules 1, 6 and 8: cleanup belongs at the acquisition site, and function scope stays function scope. The close is wrapped in try/catch because seven cases close the connection themselves first, which pytest's teardown tolerates too.

systematic_mappings.to: patchSeam(ledgerSeams, "ledgerSchemaPath", stripped), with loadLedgerSql reading only through the seam record
systematic_mappings.why: ESM bindings resolve at link time and cannot be rebound from outside; `vi.mock` reaches importers, not intra-module calls. This reproduces Python's late binding rather than working around it (D-0014, conventions rule 5). A target-only liveness case pins that production still routes through the seam.

TypeScript has no private-to-module-but-visible-to-tests spelling. The alternative -- reimplementing the collapse rule in the test -- would make the case compare its own construction against itself instead of against the loader's rule.
better-sqlite3 returns row objects, and the column name here is literally `COUNT(*)`. `.pluck()` is the faithful reading of a one-column row without hard-coding that name.

systematic_mappings.to: a top-of-file import of SPIKE_APPLICATION_ID in the TEST file only
systematic_mappings.why: The deferred import exists so `canary` carries no import-time dependency on `control_plane`. In this port that dependency is the test's, not the module's (`src/canary/ledger.ts` imports nothing from `control_plane`), so a static import in the test file is the honest spelling and the protected property still holds.

An unconfigured better-sqlite3 handle with `unsafeMode(true)` -- the testkit's `raw()` -- is what corresponds to Python's `sqlite3.connect`, which has no defensive mode. It also closes on test finish, which matters on Windows.

target_only_tests.why: target-only -- the built package carries routing_ledger.sql byte for byte: `LEDGER_SCHEMA_PATH` resolves beside `ledger.js`, so a build that emits the JavaScript and forgets the `.sql` ships a module in which the ledger can be neither created nor opened -- and every other case in this file passes, because they all run against the source tree. Byte-for-byte rather than merely present, because the fingerprint hashes these exact bytes and a normalised line ending would make the packaged build refuse every ledger the source build wrote. Python packages data files differently, so the source has no counterpart. Guarded so a missing build reports 'run npm run build' rather than failing confusingly. target-only -- loadLedgerSql reads the schema path through the seam record: Required by conventions rule 5: a seam that production stopped routing through rots into a decoration, and the case that patches it would then be testing nothing. Pins that the CONTENT loadLedgerSql returns is the patched file's. target-only -- a reopened ledger also refuses INSERT OR REPLACE: The source exercises OR REPLACE only through the create path's connection, so `recursive_triggers = ON` could be applied on that path alone and the whole ported belt would stay green -- while every long-running process, which opens rather than creates, ran without the guarantee. The pragma is per-connection; this asserts the open path carries it. Named as a required addition by the design review. target-only -- a trigger dropped by a foreign connection is caught at reopen: The ported case drops the trigger through the module's own connection, which is the one thing that cannot happen in production: the writer that damages a store is a hand-run `sqlite3` session or another process. This does the damage through a raw handle and asserts the fingerprint catches it on the way back in -- which a cached expected fingerprint, or a verify-on-create-only design, would lose. Named as a required addition by the design review. target-only -- the ledger stays on the rollback journal, created and reopened: The design constraint that this module must not build on `src/sqlite/open.ts`'s `openDatabase` comes down to one pragma: `openDatabase` sets `journal_mode = WAL`. Nothing else in the belt can see WAL (measured -- see failOnPurpose), so without this case a shared opener could be substituted and 32 of 33 tests would stay green. Both halves are asserted (the journal mode on a created AND a reopened connection, and no sidecars while a written-to connection is open) because either alone is satisfiable by accident. target-only -- a refused open leaves the file byte identical and makes no sidecar: 'Verification only reads, so a refused file is left exactly as it was found' is stated in the source's docstring and asserted by no source case. Catches a verification that repairs or otherwise writes (verified by mutation). It does NOT catch WAL -- that is the previous case's job -- and the file comment says so. target-only -- a foreign connection cannot move a started run's owner: D-0405's measurement, as a case. `recursive_triggers` is per-connection, so an ordinary `new Database(path)` -- every caller that has not read ledger.ts -- ran `INSERT OR REPLACE INTO run_owner` against SQLite's default of OFF and the implicit conflict-resolution DELETE fired no trigger: measured, the owner moved from synthetic_v1 to interlock and the tampered ledger then passed `openRoutingLedger` in full, because ownership is data and no verification rung reads it. The case asserts the foreign handle's pragma really is 0 before it tampers, so it cannot pass by inheriting the module's discipline, and re-opens through the module afterwards to pin the half nothing checked. target-only -- a foreign connection cannot rewrite the routing history: the same hole one relation along, where an edited row would additionally destroy the rollback's own evidence and still be reported as append-only by `compareAcrossRollback`, which compares what it is given. target-only -- the replacement guard defers to the row's own CHECKs: load-bearing for `routeRunStart`, not a curiosity. SQLite runs BEFORE INSERT triggers ahead of constraint checking, so a guard whose WHEN were a bare EXISTS(...) would answer a MALFORMED duplicate with a trigger refusal, and since D-0406 classifies SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER as an already-routed conflict the broken write would be reported as an idempotent success -- exactly what the ported `an idempotent retry does not absorb a validation failure` forbids. Measured: with the WHEN clause reduced to EXISTS(...) alone, this case and that ported case both go red. target-only -- a negative sequence cannot brick ordinary appends: SQLite gives NEW.decision_seq the value -1 in a BEFORE INSERT trigger when the insert supplies no sequence -- the manual says 'undefined', and measured on SQLite 3.53.4 it is -1 on an empty table and a populated one alike. The replacement guard asks whether NEW.decision_seq is already present, so a row sitting AT -1 would make every ordinary append look like a replacement and be refused: a working ledger bricked by a value only an out-of-band writer could have put there. Found by the review gate on this change and reproduced; its second round then found the other direction, since SQLite assigns an omitted rowid as MAX + 1 and a stored -2 therefore makes the next auto-assigned sequence -1 -- the sentinel as the value being WRITTEN. `CHECK (decision_seq >= 0)` closes both at once. The case drives -1 and -2 and asserts both halves of the property, the refusal and that appends still append afterwards, because the CHECK could be deleted and only the second half would notice. target-only -- zero is still an ordinary sequence the ordering trigger judges: the reserved half stops at zero on purpose. The ported `a decision cannot be back filled behind the newest` inserts sequence 0 and matches `appended in order`, the ORDERING trigger's sentence; a CHECK swallowing 0 first would leave that case green while it asserted something else. This pins which constraint speaks for 0, so the boundary cannot be widened without a red test.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `createRoutingLedger`'s cleanup path calls `connection.close()` unguarded before `rmSync`. A close that itself throws aborts the cleanup, leaves the half-created file on disk, and surfaces the close error instead of the original.
inherited_limitations.why: Python's `except BaseException: connection.close(); target.unlink(missing_ok=True); raise` has exactly this shape. Guarding it here would make the port quietly better than the source on a path no test reaches, which is the kind of silent divergence a parity port exists to avoid. `control_plane/schema.ts` carries the same inherited shape with the same comment.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The `integrity_check` failure message interpolates a Python-repr-shaped rendering (`[('ok',)]`) built by a local `renderRow`/`renderRows` pair, duplicated from `control_plane/schema.ts` rather than shared.
inherited_limitations.why: Python interpolates the repr of a list of 1-tuples and there is no natural TS equivalent, so the rendering is a deliberate choice rather than a translation (it should be pinned in the parity ledger). It is duplicated rather than imported because `schema.ts` does not export it and widening that module's surface for a message would couple two modules that hash different databases for different reasons. No ported case asserts this string -- no fixture in this belt reaches the integrity_check rung.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `verify` runs before `configureLedgerConnection`, so `integrity_check` and `foreign_key_check` execute with `foreign_keys` and `recursive_triggers` at SQLite's defaults (both OFF).
inherited_limitations.why: That is the source's order exactly. `foreign_key_check` is unaffected by the `foreign_keys` pragma, so the dangling-reference case still lands; changing the order would be a divergence with no test behind it.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: `create_routing_ledger` applies the DDL before the pragmas are configured, so `executescript`/`exec` runs with foreign keys and recursive triggers off.
inherited_limitations.why: The source's order. It is DDL only, so nothing observable depends on it, but it is preserved rather than tidied.

inherited_limitations.behaviour: The schema fingerprint query filters with `name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'`, in which `_` is a single-character wildcard rather than a literal underscore, so an object named `sqliteX` and similar would also be excluded from the fingerprint.
inherited_limitations.why: Carried verbatim from `ledger.py`, and load-bearing: the fingerprint hashes exactly the rows this query returns, so narrowing the pattern (to `LIKE 'sqlite\_%' ESCAPE '\'`) would change every fingerprint this build computes and make it disagree with a ledger written by interlock's. `src/control_plane/schema.ts` carries the same pattern for the same reason. Raised as [P2] by the review gate; a parity port cannot narrow it unilaterally.

divergences.behaviour: continuo's routing ledger DDL carries two BEFORE INSERT triggers interlock's does not: `run_owner_is_never_replaced` and `routing_decision_is_never_replaced`. They refuse an INSERT whose key is already present, which is what `INSERT OR REPLACE` is, and they fire ahead of conflict resolution -- so the refusal holds on a connection where `recursive_triggers` is OFF, which is every connection this package did not hand out.
divergences.note: interlock's DDL concedes this hole in a comment and D-0022 would have let the port disclose and leave it; D-0023 withdrew that answer, and D-0405 scheduled the repair as its own change rather than letting it land inside the belt that claimed 70/70. Measured before the repair (better-sqlite3 13.0.3, SQLite 3.53.4, 2026-08-28): a bare `new Database(path)` moved run-1's owner from synthetic_v1 to interlock in one statement, and the tampered ledger then passed `openRoutingLedger` in full -- integrity_check, application_id, user_version, table presence, schema fingerprint and foreign_key_check all hold, because ownership is data and none of those rungs reads it. Measured after (2026-08-29): the same statement is refused SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER with the pragma reading 0, and the standing row is unchanged. The guards' WHEN clauses restate the tables' own column CHECKs so that a malformed row is left to the CHECK rather than masked by a 'you may not replace this' refusal; D-0406 explains why that is load-bearing rather than tidy. One more line of DDL belongs to the same repair and is called out separately because it is not a trigger: `CHECK (decision_seq >= 0)` on routing_decision. SQLite's value for NEW.decision_seq in a BEFORE INSERT trigger that supplies no sequence is documented as undefined and measured as -1, so without reserving it a row stored at -1 would make every ordinary append look to the guard like a replacement. The whole negative half is reserved rather than the single value, because SQLite assigns an omitted rowid as MAX + 1: a stored -2 makes the next auto-assigned sequence -1, the sentinel arriving as the value being written rather than the value being matched. Reserving it keeps the guard exact rather than making it guess whether a sequence was supplied, and any other value the undefined case might take is harmless on its own terms -- it matches no row, so the guard stands aside, which is the right answer for an insert that cannot collide. Zero remains an ordinary sequence number, deliberately: the back-filling `routing_decision_is_appended_in_order` refuses is what the ported case pins, by inserting 0 and matching `appended in order`, and a CHECK swallowing 0 first would change what that case asserts. Raised as [P2] by the review gate on this change, in two rounds -- the stored sentinel first, the assigned one second.
divergences.parity_cost: Two of the 27 translated cases in this file change the message they match, from `never deleted` to `never replaced`, and are recorded as `adapted` above with interlock's own `match=` quoted in each reason. Nothing else moves: the same statements are refused, the same post-state reads hold, and the other 25 cases are untouched. On every path interlock's DDL refuses, continuo's refuses too -- the divergence is only in which trigger speaks and therefore in what it says. Where interlock ADMITS the write (a foreign connection) continuo refuses it, and continuo is authoritative there: interlock is frozen, so this is where the guarantee can be made true. The reserved negative half is likewise invisible to interlock's suite: no source case inserts a negative decision_seq, the lowest one any of them uses is 0, and interlock's own DDL cannot reach the sentinel at all because it has no BEFORE INSERT trigger on this table to reach it with.
divergences.evidence: test/canary/ledger.test.ts::store enforcement on every connection (target-only) > the three target-only cases named in target_only_tests.why, plus the two adapted cases above. The DDL's own comments carry the reasoning at the trigger definitions.
